result.summary: The poet continues describing the decorated shield made by Hephaestus for Heracles. Scenes include a harbour with dolphins and a fisherman, Perseus fleeing the Gorgons, a besieged city with the Fates and Darkness of Death, a city at a wedding festival, and scenes of farming, vintage, hunting and a chariot race.

scenes.title: Harbour with dolphins and fisherman
scenes.summary: The shield shows a tin harbour with silver dolphins chasing bronze fishes while a fisherman waits with a net.

scenes.title: Perseus flees the Gorgons
scenes.summary: Golden Perseus flies with winged sandals and the cap of Hades, carrying the Gorgon's head, while the other Gorgons chase him.
scenes.stakes: Perseus is pursued by the Gorgons who long to seize him.

scenes.title: Battle over a town, Fates
scenes.summary: Men fight to defend or sack a town while elders pray and the grim Fates and Darkness of Death seize the fallen.
scenes.stakes: The townsfolk risk death and the sack of their city.

scenes.title: City at peace: wedding
scenes.summary: A city with seven golden gates celebrates a wedding with torches, song, pipes and dance.

scenes.title: Farming, vintage, sports, race
scenes.summary: Riders, ploughmen, reapers, grape gatherers, boxers, hunters and charioteers are shown, with a golden tripod as the prize.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet for the lame smith god.
Demeter stands for grain by metonymy.

notable_quotes.reason: Marvelling at Hephaestus's craft: Perseus appears to fly unsupported.

analysis.text: The shield contrasts war and death with festival, farming and play, presenting a whole world of human life.
The description imitates the shield of Achilles in the Iliad, showing the epic tradition of ekphrasis.

legacy.text: The passage belongs to the tradition of the described shield, which runs from Homer's Achilles shield to Virgil's shield of Aeneas.

fun_facts.text: The Shield of Heracles is ascribed to Hesiod in antiquity, but modern scholars generally doubt his authorship.

language_notes.text: "Mute" fishes: silent, voiceless; a standard descriptive touch for fish in Greek poetry.
"The famous Lame One" is Hephaestus, the smith god, referred to by an epithet instead of his name.
A cross-belt is a baldric, a strap worn diagonally over the shoulder to carry a sword.
The cap of Hades made its wearer invisible. Perseus borrowed it to approach the Gorgons unseen. The number 1804 is a stray page marker.
Adamant is a legendary unbreakable metal; here it describes the pale surface of the shield on which the Gorgons run.
"Like living beings" is odd: the women are figures worked in metal, so the poet likens the images to real women in their lifelike grief.
Tartarus is the gloomy lowest region of the underworld; here it is used loosely alongside Hades for the place of the dead.
Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos are the three Fates, who spun, measured and cut the thread of each human life.
"Darkness of Death" translates a personified figure, Achlys, a spirit of mist and misery associated with dying.
"Well-wheeled car" means a well-made wagon or chariot in which the bride was conveyed to her husband's house in the wedding procession.
"Tunics girt up" means tunics belted high so the legs were free for work.
"Cars" is an old word for ears of grain, not vehicles. The translator's spelling reflects older usage.
"Demeter's grain" uses the goddess's name for grain itself, a metonymy common in Greek poetry.
"Turned black 1805" contains a stray printed date, a text error; it likely means the grapes were ripening dark.
"Liquor" here means the freshly pressed grape juice or wine.
"Hard set" means hard pressed or intensely engaged in the contest.
"Naves" are the hubs of the wheels, where the axle passes through.

context_notes.text: Perseus, son of Zeus and Danae, beheaded the Gorgon Medusa. Her head turned onlookers to stone.
Medusa's two immortal sisters, Stheno and Euryale, chased Perseus after he killed her.
Hephaestus was the smith god, who made the shield's metalwork; the poet reminds us the whole scene is his craftsmanship.
Elders too old to fight stayed outside the gates and prayed, a common picture of a besieged town.
Hephaestus was the divine smith who forged the shield, so the golden vine is a god's craftsmanship.
A tripod was a three-legged cauldron or stand, a typical prize in Greek games and a valuable gift.

literary_notes.text: The tin harbour that seems to heave with waves makes a static metal object look alive and moving.
Comparing Perseus's flight to thought conveys extreme speed in a few words.
The ringing, clanging shield makes the sound of the chase audible, adding noise to a silent artwork.
Fear is imagined as a being quaking upon the Gorgons' heads, making terror a visible presence.
The Fates are shown as snarling, fanged beasts thirsting for blood, turning fate into predatory violence.
Piled grim physical details of hunger and decay make Death's spirit repulsive and vivid.
The golden-gated city of festival follows the scene of war and death, setting peace against slaughter on the same shield.
Sound, light and movement of pipes, lyres, echo and dance create a lively picture of joy.
The balanced clause about hunters and hares both being eager makes the chase seem alive, suspended between pursuit and escape.
The clattering cars and shrieking wheel hubs bring sound into a silent metal image, making the scene vivid.
The contest is endless and no one wins, so the prize is displayed but never gained, a frozen moment of art.
